item.description: By Adegboyega Adeleye The Kwankwasiyya movement has accused the African Democratic Congress (ADC) and former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar of being unclear about what they would offer Nigerians, saying the party was relying on the presidential flagbearers of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Peter Obi and Rabiu Musa Kwankwaso, to advance Atiku’s 2027 presidential ambition. The movement’s spokesperson, Dr Habibu Sale Mohammed, made the allegation on Daily Trust TV’s Day Break on Monday, while responding to the NDC vice-presidential candidate’s statement over the weekend, where he ruled out an alliance with the ADC. Mohammed said parties should present their ideas and capabilities to voters rather than blame their prospects on politicians who decline to join them. “The politics should be played, often presenting yourself, your ideas, your capacities and capabilities for Nigerians to make the right choice. It is not about causing Nigerians to one angle,” he said. He alleged that the ADC had calculated that having Kwankwaso and Obi on its side would put Atiku in contention, whether or not Nigerians considered him the right choice. “I believe that ADC have already made its own calculation that with Kwankwaso and Obi on their side, Atiku will be there, whether he deserved to be there or not, whether he is a better alternative or not, whether he is someone others truly wanted to be there or not, and they are still crying, simply because they are not clear as to what exactly they want to offer Nigerians, and to us, the survival of democracy is the most important thing here,” he said. item.title: Dollar to Naira exchange rate today, October 20, 2026
item.description: The dollar-to-naira exchange rate remained relatively stable around the ₦1,330 level in the official market on Tuesday, October 20, 2026, while the parallel market continued to quote higher rates for buyers seeking physical US dollars. The latest available foreign exchange data put the official Nigerian Foreign Exchange Market (NFEM) reference rate at approximately ₦1,332 per dollar. In the parallel market, Bureau De Change (BDC) operators quoted varying rates depending on location and transaction size. As of Tuesday morning, the indicative rates are: Official NFEM rate: approximately ₦1,332 per dollar, based on the latest available reference data. Parallel-market buying rate: around ₦1,365 per dollar. Parallel-market selling rate: around ₦1,380 per dollar. The parallel-market figures are indicative quotations and may differ among dealers. How much is $100 to naira today? At the indicative rates, $100 is worth approximately ₦133,200 at the official reference rate and ₦138,000 at the parallel-market selling rate. The difference reflects the premium often paid by individuals who obtain dollars through unofficial market channels rather than the official foreign exchange window. The gap between the two markets affects importers, international travellers, students paying overseas tuition and businesses with dollar-denominated obligations. Nigerians planning foreign exchange transactions should confirm the applicable rate with their banks or licensed Bureau De Change operators, as prices can change during the day. Read Also: “Government people up there can afford 22-year-old brandy, but this is what we can afford,” he said, pointing to a sachet. “Many drivers here cannot start their day without one or two sachets. The danger was never a secret. Health experts warned repeatedly that sachet alcohol encourages excessive and reckless consumption because it is cheap, portable, and sold everywhere. You find it at motor parks, markets and street corners. The ban was not about punishing pleasure; it was about saving lives. Yet in Cross River State, from the bustling Watt Market in Calabar, to the timber market in Ogoja, from Ikom motor park to the quiet streets of Okpoma in Yala Local Government Area, the banned beverages still dangle openly from ropes and shop rafters. Hawkers push carts loaded with them through motor parks, and even children run errands carrying the deadly pouches from place to place. There is no fear of arrest, no hiding, no shame. The law exists on paper, but on the ground, it is business as usual. At Calabar’s Watt Market, a trader who gave her name as Iquo laughed off the idea of a ban. “I never hear say government ban this thing,” she said, even as she admitted that enforcement agents had raided her stall a few times. “When they come, I beg them and give them something small, they go release my goods.” Her confession tells its own story: the ban is real, but so is the corruption that quietly kills it. She sells the alcohol in several brands from her stand near the motor park where motorcycle riders pick passengers, and she insisted she had no other business to fall back on. In Ogoja, around the timber market, Egbe Anderson, who openly sells the drinks, asked a reporter a question that stung: “If government is serious, why are supply vans still coming every day from Lagos, Port Harcourt, Aba, and Onitsha? New brands are coming out every day, and you are talking about ban. Ban what?” His question exposes the broken chain of enforcement — while shops are raided, manufacturers and distributors continue to flood the market with impunity. A traditional ruler in Okpoma, Ogamode Onah, offered a rare voice of reason. “I support the ban totally,” he said. “These boys take these drinks with kolos and other dangerous things and cause trouble. Every day, we see accidents on the road because they drink before riding okada or driving. Young people cannot even work on the farm without taking these things. Let those enforcing the ban be serious.” His words echo the pain of communities that bury young men almost every week. At the NAFDAC office in Calabar, an official explained that the journey to the ban began in 2018, when NAFDAC, the Federal Ministry of Health, and industry stakeholders signed an agreement giving manufacturers a five-year moratorium to phase out sachet alcohol by January 31, 2024. Enforcement began in February 2024 but was extended after manufacturers appealed. On January 1, 2026, the full ban finally became active, backed by a Senate resolution and NAFDAC enforcement. Since July 2026, the agency has been conducting nationwide “shop-and-market mop-up” operations. “So what you see on the streets and markets are illegal,” the official said. The question now is whether the government has the will to match its words with action. A law that exists only in press statements and official gazettes cannot save the young man in Ikom who drinks before driving, or the teenager in Calabar who mixes sachet gin with hard drugs. The ban on sachet alcohol was written in blood — the blood of accident victims, of wasted youths, of families destroyed by cheap addiction. Until enforcement becomes real, until corrupt officers stop collecting bribes, and until communities and traditional rulers join the fight, the killer in the sachet will keep flowing freely through Cross River State and beyond. item.title: Jesse fire disaster: 28 years after, community still cries for justice
item.description: •The dead were victims of alleged corporate, govt negligence — Judith; •Demands national monument in their honour; •Govt, oil giants should establish Idjerhe tragedy memorial museum — Dr. Egbedi; •Support our quest for justice — Ovie of Idjerhe Kingdom By Jimitota Onoyume & Paul Olayemi For 28 years, the people of Jesse community in Ethiope West Local Government Area of Delta State have carried the pain of the loss of about 1,082 natives who perished in a petrol fire incident that was no fault of theirs in Atiwor community. Read Also: Untold story of pipeline fire explosion that killed over 22 persons Last Saturday, October 17, the people of the area and guests from far and near gathered in their large numbers for a memorial ceremony at the scene of the incident in Atiwor community, Jesse kingdom. •The Ovie of Idjerhe kingdom, His Majesty, King Monday Obukowho Whiskey, Udurhie 1 (middle), flanked by his chiefs, Convener of the memorial event, Lady Judith Nwachukwu, and community folks, offers prayers in front of the mass grave, at the scene of the Jesse fire disaster. It would be recalled that on October 17, 1998, a 16-inch high-pressure pipeline conveying petrol from Warri to the Kaduna refinery, owned by the Nigerian National Petroleum Corporation (NNPC), suffered a leakage. The petrol content spread rapidly across the area. Till date, no official cause of the incident has been reported on the pipeline built in the 1970s, which had suffered from ageing and neglect. They were consumed in a fire explosion that suddenly occurred at the scene. Some said a lighted cigarette some distance away may have caused the fire. The painful incident, later known globally as the Jesse fire disaster, was the first time in the country that Nigerians in such large numbers were consumed in a petrol fire incident. Some have renamed that single largest industrial disaster a Holocaust. It attracted the attention of the globe, with international media houses visiting the scene to capture gory pictures of charred remains of corpses. The military Head of State then, General Abdusalami Abubakar, also flew to the community with top members of his cabinet to commiserate with the people at the scene. Chief convener of the memorial event, Lady Judith Ojevwe Nwachukwu (nee Deniran) in her welcome address, recalled that the fire incident remained the deadliest single industrial disaster ever recorded in the country, stressing that it was due largely to.alleged corporate negligence and zero maintenance culture of the Federal Government and the operating oil firm. “The community came to national and global consciousness after the tragic October 1998 pipeline explosion that consumed 1,082 lives. That tragedy remains one of the deadliest industrial disasters the world has ever witnessed,” she said. “We note that the Idjerhe pipeline explosion was not an accident; it was an inevitable event owing to corporate negligence and zero maintenance culture of both the Federal Government and the oil multinational companies that laid the pipes. It was the rupture of the 16-inch pipeline conveying crude to Kaduna that led to the explosion,“ she added. She further demanded that the Federal Government immortalise the victims by naming an institution and a monument after them. “To remember those victims, we demand a monument and an institution to be named in their honour. We also demand regular maintenance of the mass grave to serve as a historical site for generations,” she said. Dr. Johnson Dudu, who gave the first lecture, called for collaboration among the people of Jesse for post-recovery in the area after the sad incident. “We need the collaboration to bring about the post-disaster recovery. It requires collaboration to achieve. We must communicate effectively the needs of the community, build relationships even beyond the government. We must make specific requests,” he said. Dr. Mrs. Martha Egbedi, who gave the second lecture, called on the government and other relevant stakeholders to set up an Idjerhe tragedy memorial museum and environmental learning centre where students will come to learn about pipeline safety. She also urged the government and oil companies to conduct a full integrity audit of pipelines running through the Jesse community to avoid another disaster, adding that youths from the area should be employed. “In 1998, we were told it was sabotage. In 2024, the National Oil Spill Detection and Response Agency (NOSDRA) still recorded over 500 spills in the Niger-Delta. When will it end? We demand a full integrity audit of all pipelines in Idjerhe kingdom and a community pipeline surveillance model that employs our own youths, not outsiders. Prevention is cheaper than mass burial,” she said. “Beneath our feet are those buried here from no fault of theirs. If we remember, we must remember correctly. We remember that their families were not compensated. A celebrated environmentalist called it a holocaust. Our people were not criminals. They died because of the failure of the state. Idjerhe women became widows overnight. Our women have carried this pain for 28 years,” she lamented. Gibson Ikanone, who gave the last paper, called for what he termed a diplomatic belligerence approach to get justice for the memories of those consumed in the inferno. He charged the leadership of the Urhobo Progress Union (UPU) to also join the demand for justice for the area. Others who spoke at the event included former member of the House of Representatives representing Ethiope Federal Constituency, Chief Halims Agoda; the lawmaker representing Ethiope West State Constituency in the state House of Assembly, Hon. Achoja Blessing; the Otota of Idjerhe Kingdom, High Chief James Onosia Obriki; and the Unogbrogodo of the kingdom, Chief Solomon Ojaraife, who all lamented the sad incident in their separate speeches. Agoda recalled how he confronted the Head of State, General Abubakar, over the incident when he visited, saying the Head of State, who understood the pain of the community, ordered his soldiers to be civil that day. Agoda echoed the call for justice for the area. The Ovie of Idjerhe Kingdom, His Majesty King Monday Obukohwo Whiskey Ph.D., Udurhie 1, who later led the community to offer prayers and light candles at the mass grave of those consumed, appealed for greater support from stakeholders across the Niger Delta to get justice for the people of Jesse. He recalled that he was a practising Journalist when the sad incident occurred in 1998, adding that when he rushed to the scene that day, he was overwhelmed by the charred remains of his natives on the ground. “I was a Journalist with a national newspaper when it happened. I was overwhelmed by what I saw when I came to the scene. I had to put myself together before I could do anything,” he recalled. “As a media practitioner, I helped other places in the Niger Delta to fight for justice for their areas . I appeal to you all to help me and my people to fight for justice “ he urged. He also expressed gratitude to the convener of the memorial programme, Lady Judith, and the special guests from the Urhobo Arts Heritage Company Limited led by Professor Godini Godwin Darah, who was represented by the Secretary of the group, Felix Kporhotor. item.title: National grid crashes 81% to 675MW, as 9 plants go off
item.description: By Obas Esiedesa, Abuja Nigeria’s grid electricity supply crashed by 81.5 per cent to 675 megawatts (MW) at 1pm on Monday from 3,647MW, following a drop in the number of power plants supplying the national grid from 21 to 2. Read Also: Buhari: If a general couldn’t wipe out insecurity, spare Tinubu — Yari The development prompted electricity distribution companies, including Abuja Electricity Distribution Company (AEDC) and Ikeja Electric, to issue public notices informing customers of supply constraints linked to challenges on the national grid. Data from the Nigerian Independent System Operator (NISO) showed that 21 power plants were supplying electricity to the grid before the incident at noon, when total generation stood at 3,647MW. However, by 1pm, the number of plants on the grid had dropped to 12, while electricity supply plunged to 675MW, representing a loss of 2,972MW within one hour. The plants that went offline included Azura, Egbin, Jebba and Kainji hydroelectric power plants. The sharp decline followed relatively higher supply levels earlier in the day, with the grid recording 4,331MW at 1am and 4,458MW at 6am. Supply subsequently fell to 3,647MW by noon before experiencing the steep drop at 1pm. Electricity supply later recovered to 2,150MW by 5pm, representing an improvement of 1,475MW from the 1pm level, although it remained significantly below the morning peak. In a public notice issued on Monday, AEDC informed customers that electricity supply from the Transmission Company of Nigeria (TCN) had been interrupted due to a grid-related challenge. The company said TCN’s technical team was working to restore grid stability, adding that power supply was gradually being restored to its feeders. “We assure you that efforts are ongoing to restore full supply across our franchise area as soon as the situation permits,” AEDC said, while apologising for the inconvenience caused by the interruption. Similarly, Ikeja Electric attributed reduced electricity supply across its network to a shortfall in the volume of power allocated to it from the national grid. In its notice to customers, the distribution company said it was engaging relevant stakeholders to improve available supply. It added that it would continue to distribute the electricity received from the grid as efficiently and equitably as possible. However, NISO said it had stabilised the national grid following multiple trippings on the 330-kilovolt (kV) transmission network. In a statement on Monday, the system operator said the incident occurred at approximately 12:40pm on October 19, 2026. It said it immediately implemented corrective measures in collaboration with TCN to stabilise the power system and restore normal operations. According to NISO, restoration efforts had been successfully completed and the national grid had returned to normal operation. Data from the Nigerian Independent System Operator (NISO) showed that 21 power plants were supplying electricity to the grid before the incident at noon, when total generation stood at 3,647MW. However, by 1pm, the number of plants on the grid had dropped to 12, while electricity supply plunged to 675MW, representing a loss of 2,972MW within one hour. The plants that went offline included Azura, Egbin, Jebba and Kainji hydroelectric power plants. The sharp decline followed relatively higher supply levels earlier in the day, with the grid recording 4,331MW at 1am and 4,458MW at 6am. Supply subsequently fell to 3,647MW by noon before experiencing the steep drop at 1pm. Electricity supply later recovered to 2,150MW by 5pm, representing an improvement of 1,475MW from the 1pm level, although it remained significantly below the morning peak. In a public notice issued on Monday, AEDC informed customers that electricity supply from the Transmission Company of Nigeria (TCN) had been interrupted due to a grid-related challenge. The company said TCN’s technical team was working to restore grid stability, adding that power supply was gradually being restored to its feeders. “We assure you that efforts are ongoing to restore full supply across our franchise area as soon as the situation permits,” AEDC said, while apologising for the inconvenience caused by the interruption. Similarly, Ikeja Electric attributed reduced electricity supply across its network to a shortfall in the volume of power allocated to it from the national grid. In its notice to customers, the distribution company said it was engaging relevant stakeholders to improve available supply. It added that it would continue to distribute the electricity received from the grid as efficiently and equitably as possible. However, NISO said it had stabilised the national grid following multiple trippings on the 330-kilovolt (kV) transmission network. In a statement on Monday, the system operator said the incident occurred at approximately 12:40pm on October 19, 2026. It said it immediately implemented corrective measures in collaboration with TCN to stabilise the power system and restore normal operations. According to NISO, restoration efforts had been successfully completed and the national grid had returned to normal operation. The operator clarified that the incident affected only a section of the grid, contrary to unverified reports and claims. item.title: 40th memorial: Media icons pay tributes to ‘Dele Giwa’s Granite Journalism’
item.description: •Giwa had premonition of his death — Osoba By Sebastine Obasi Media icons yesterday converged on the Nigerian Institute of Journalism, NIJ, Ogba, Lagos, where they paid tributes to Dele Giwa, one of Nigeria’s journalism icons. The occasion was the book presentation to mark the 40th anniversary of the death of Dele Giwa, Co-founder of Newswatch magazine, who was assassinated through a parcel bomb on October 19, 1986. The event drew media icons and eminent Nigerians such as former governor, Segun Osoba, Nduka Obaigbena, publisher, ThisDay, Newspapers, Yemi Ogunbiyi, former managing director, Daily Times, Biodun Shobanjo, former Chaiman, Insight Communications, Ralp Akinfeleye, emeritus professor, University of Lagos, Nosa Igiebor, Co-founder, Tell Magazine, Chuka Momah, ace columnist, Gbenga Adefaye, Provost, Nigerian Institute of Journalism, Funmi and Aisha, Dele Giwa’s wife and daughter, respectively. Founder and Publisher of Vanguard Newspapers, Sam Amuka, who was the Chairman of the occasion, described late Dele Giwa, Co-founder, Newswatch magazine, as a true legend and patriotic Nigerian journalist during his lifetime. Amuka stated this at the book presentation on Dele Giwa’s Granite Journalism, held at the Kesington Adebutu Auditorium, NIJ, Ogba, Lagos. Amuka, who recalled Giwa’s popular saying, ‘’protest pays” also stated that it takes a legend to propound such theory, which has proven to be right, especially in the Nigerian context. For him, though Giwa died at 39, his legacy lives. He enjoined the audience, as well as other Nigerians to buy the book, which he said, it worth reading. Also, speaking, Ray Ekpu, Co-founder of Newswatch magazine, stated that Giwa was a blessing to Nigeria’s journalism, as he brought to bear, his high intellect and engaging investigation into the profession. Ekpu described Giwa’s untimely death by a parcel bomb, as deeply devastating to the Newswatch family, who made humanly efforts to unravel the killers without success. Going down memory lane, former governor, Segun Osoba, who was managing director of Times, stated how a day before his death, Giwa had complained to his colleagues at an event at Victoria Island that security personnel were after his life. An urgent meeting was arranged between the journalists and Augustus Aikhomu, then Chief of General Staff, who assured them that he would investigate the matter. Osoba commended Giwa’s courage and sense of patriotism. For Yemi Ogunbiyi, former managing director of Daily Times, Giwa was a remarkable human being, who added colour and vibrancy to Nigeria’s journalism. For Biodun Shobanjo, public relations czar, Dele Giwa was an enigma, as he was larger than life. “We should all take pride in having Giwa as a husband, colleague, riend and fantastic journalistic,” he added. Aisha DeleGiwa’s daughter, stated that though he was one year old, when the father died, the stories told about him by her mother and all what she has read made her believe that Giwa died a marty

item.title: With subsidy, Naira’ll exchange at N4,000/$ — Oyedele
item.description: *I’ve no regret on subsidy removal, we can’t go back to Egypt — Tinubu *ADC takes on Oyedele over N4,000/$ claim *Ask him to provide evidence, stop using fear to discourage debate *Economy would have collapsed without Tinubu’s reforms, says Shettima *Assures food prices’ll come down soon By Clifford Ndujihe, Johnbosco Agbakwuru & Luminous Jannamike LAGOS — The Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Taiwo Oyedele, has warned Nigerians against returning to petrol subsidy. Read Also: Subsidy removal: I’ve no regret, we can’t go back to Egypt — Tinubu Oyedele said the return could trigger capital flight, undermine investor confidence and push the naira to N3,000, N3,500, or even N4,000 per dollar. He disclosed this at a press briefing of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Thailand, yesterday. In a quick counter, the Presidential Campaign Council, PCC, of the African Democratic Congress, ADC, challenged the minister to produce models showing that giving Nigerians fuel subsidy will hurt the Naira, adding that the Federal Government is discouraging debate on fuel subsidy removal through fear mongering. ADC presidential candidate, Alhaji Atiku Abubakar, has promised a return to fuel subsidy if elected, to cushion the hardship faced by the citizenry. Oyedele’s argument The minister said investors had repeatedly questioned whether government would abandon its reforms ahead of the next election cycle. Oyedele, who ruled out reversing the government’s economic reforms, maintained that any signal that President Bola Tinubu’s administration is contemplating reinstating subsidy will immediately affect financial markets, raise borrowing costs and worsen economic pressures on households. “In all the meetings I have had, I came to a conclusion that the markets, including the domestic market, which you can read from the capital market, and the international market, have largely written off the opposition in Nigeria as being unserious. “If, for any reason, the President were to say we are merely considering the return of fuel subsidy, capital would react immediately. Air fares would struggle, the naira would come under severe pressure, potentially moving towards N3,000, N3,500 or even N4,000. The very fuel people want subsidised would become far more expensive in naira terms,” he said. Oyedele warned that capital flight could extend beyond foreign investors, as wealthy Nigerians, business owners and middle-class investors might also seek refuge in dollars, further increasing demand for foreign exchange. He stressed that ordinary Nigerians will ultimately bear the consequences through higher import costs, rising prices and increased economic hardship. The minister also rejected the description of the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited’s temporary reduction in petrol retail margins as a return to subsidy, explaining that it is a commercial decision rather than a payment funded by public resources.

In the recent changes at INEC, Mrs Oluyemi Titilayo Adeyemi-Showunmi, formerly the Administrative Secretary of the commission’s Lagos State office, was redeployed as the Director of Electoral Operations at the commission. She is the wife of Segun Showunmi, a spokesman for the Tinubu/Shettima 2027 Presidential Campaign Council. Prof. Mustapha Aliu, identified as an elder brother of Sokoto State Governor, Ahmed Aliyu, who is seeking a second term on the platform of the All Progressives Congress (APC), has also been nominated as an INEC commissioner. According to reports, Isah Magaji Gummi, who previously headed the Electoral Operations Department, was redeployed to the Voter Registry Department. The Electoral Operations Department plays a key role in election planning and implementation, including the coordination of polling arrangements, deployment of election materials and management of personnel involved in electoral operations. Although the director of the department does not independently determine election results, the responsibilities attached to the office have drawn attention to the redeployment and calls for INEC to explain the considerations behind the decision. Adeyemi-Showunmi’s redeployment has sparked debate among civil society organisations and on social media over transparency, political neutrality and public confidence in the electoral body. Former director of voter education at INEC, Mr Nick Dazang, when contacted said, it would be wrong for the Commission to pretend that appointing someone that close to a sitting governor who is contesting elections has no implications. “The person may be eminently qualified but I have profound misgivings if he can discharge or execute his office as Resident Electoral Commissioner with the professionalism, neutrality and impartiality that the office demands. On the redeployment of Sowunmi wife, he said in the time past, and oblivious of the closeness/proximity of INEC officials to certain politically exposed persons, INEC officials on their merit, had been inadvertently assigned to roles/tasks that put them in difficult positions which complicated the Commission’s core values of impartiality and neutrality. He said In such circumstances, and in deference to its core values, INEC has demonstrated sensitivity by not posting such deserving officials to these positions. “It is likely that the Commission may not be aware or cognizant of the said officer’s relationship with a prominent politician. “But once this is established, and its attention is called to this reality, it should promptly do the needful, namely: not to put the officer in a position that compromises the Commission’s principles of neutrality and provision of a level playing field to all contestants. In the prevailing circumstance, the officer should be directed to recuse herself. This will allay fears, rightly or wrongly, that she has been procured to deliberately confer an advantage to any candidate(s) in the election. Either the tenure of the subsisting Director is specially extended for the period of the election, or his Deputy is directed to act in the position of Director, subject to consideration(s) of merit, federal character and the core values aforementioned,” he added. Director-General of YIAGA Africa, Samson Itodo, warned that the electoral body must ensure public confidence in the electoral process and should not take the people for granted in its appointment. On the appointment of Adeyemi-Showunmi as INEC Director of Electoral Operations, Itodo said elections are fundamentally about operations, adding that by this token, it is one of the most sensitive and consequential departments within INEC. He said, “In fact, the Electoral Operations Department is at the heart of election administration. From the recruitment and deployment of polling officials to the planning, production and distribution of election materials, as well as the operational arrangements for voting and results collation, the department plays a central role in determining how elections are conducted. “Mrs. Showunmi’s competence and professional capacity are not in doubt. However, competence alone is not sufficient for appointments to sensitive positions in election management. The independence, impartiality and perceived neutrality of those entrusted with managing elections are equally important. “Appointing individuals with strong ties to politicians in such strategic positions inevitably raises legitimate questions about impartiality and INEC independence. These concerns become even more pronounced in a climate of deep public distrust, growing fears of political capture of INEC, and politicians boldly declaring the number of votes they expect to secure before a single ballot has been cast. “At a time when public confidence in the electoral process is already fragile, appointments to critical positions within INEC should inspire confidence, not deepen suspicion. INEC must recognize that its credibility rests not only on the technical competence of its personnel but also on public confidence in INEC’s independence from partisan interests. Public confidence in the electoral process must never be taken for granted. In this instance, it is being taken for granted,” he said. Former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar was among those who first raised the alarm over the issue, demanding immediate and full transparency from INEC. In a statement issued by his Director of Strategic Communication, Phrank Shaibu, Atiku said the reported changes in the Electoral Operations Department raised serious questions that INEC must answer without delay. “Reports indicate that Director Isa Magaji Gummi was moved from Electoral Operations to the Voter Registry Department, while Mrs Oluyemi Titilayo Adeyemi-Showunmi was appointed to head Electoral Operations. Dr Lawrence Bayode has also been identified as the head of Information and Communication Technology (ICT). “These departments are at the heart of election administration. INEC must explain these decisions, publish the criteria applied and show that every appointment and redeployment followed due process, was based on merit and was free from political interference. Nigerians will not accept vague assurances on matters this serious.” Atiku said no official should be presumed compromised because of their ethnicity, background or associations. But when reported political connections or a concentration of appointments raises public concern, INEC must provide verifiable assurances that its impartiality is protected. “A government that has driven millions of Nigerians into hardship must not be allowed to turn the electoral umpire into an instrument of political survival. When sensitive election departments are reshaped and major contracts are surrounded by unanswered questions, the suspicion that a failing administration is seeking every possible advantage to cling to power will only grow. INEC must dispel that suspicion through full, immediate and verifiable disclosure,” he said. A political analyst, Professor Saleh Dauda, maintained that political undertones cannot be ruled out in the redeployment of Adeyemi-Showunmi ahead of the general elections. The PSN identified the major open drug markets in Idumota, Lagos; Head Bridge, Onitsha, Anambra State; Sabon Gari, Kano; and Ariaria, Aba, Abia State, as requiring sustained government attention under the reform. Ibrahim said the CWC initiative had recorded progress in Kano, while projects in Lagos and Anambra required continued attention to ensure their completion and effective operation. He added that Abia State Governor, Alex Otti, had promised support for the initiative in the state. He urged the Federal Government to collaborate with the affected state governments to remove administrative and other obstacles delaying the establishment and operation of the centres. According to him, effective implementation of the guidelines, alongside stronger penalties, would help strengthen the medicine supply chain and improve patient safety. The PSN president also warned against placing the responsibility for identifying fake medicines on patients, insisting that pharmacists and other qualified professionals had a critical role to play in protecting consumers. He said manufacturers conducted quality-control checks before releasing medicines to the market, while some companies had introduced product-verification systems to help detect suspected counterfeits. “It is not the job of a patient to check or confirm whether a drug is fake or not. The pharmacist that showed the drug to him should be able to check if the drug is fake or not,” he said. Ibrahim advised Nigerians to purchase medicines from registered pharmacies rather than unregulated outlets, warning that unauthorised sales of prescription medicines, including antibiotics, could expose consumers to serious health risks. He stressed the need for public education on the safe purchase and use of medicines, noting that patent medicine vendors were subject to restrictions on the products they could legally sell. On the rising cost of medicines, the PSN president said government incentives for pharmaceutical manufacturers would have limited impact unless authorities addressed the broader costs of local production. He explained that reductions in import tariffs alone might not translate into cheaper medicines if manufacturers continued to face high diesel prices, electricity costs and transportation expenses. “Unless the government takes a holistic view of the drivers of the prices of pharmaceuticals, we are not going to see any appreciable decrease in the cost of drugs,” he said. Ibrahim urged the government to consult pharmaceutical manufacturers and their industry associations before introducing policies intended to reduce medicine prices, arguing that manufacturers could provide practical insights into the factors driving production costs. He also called for stronger collaboration between government agencies responsible for natural-product research and pharmaceutical manufacturers to develop promising research findings into medicines for local use. The PSN president warned that the high cost of medicines was pushing some Nigerians away from conventional healthcare towards traditional remedies, underscoring the need to improve access to affordable and quality-assured medicines. Meanwhile, PSN National Secretary, Pharm. Gafar Madehein, cautioned Nigerians against assuming that herbal products were safe simply because they carried NAFDAC registration numbers. He explained that a registration number issued for listing purposes did not necessarily mean that a product had undergone clinical trials demonstrating its safety and efficacy. item.title: Drone Strikes Across Sudan Kill More Than 100 People
item.description: A wave of drone strikes targeting war-torn Sudan’s army-held capital Khartoum and two western areas controlled by paramilitary forces has killed more than 100 people since Sunday, according to residents, medical workers and paramilitary sources. The deadliest drone strike hit near a market on Sunday evening in Al-Dibab town in the southwestern state of West Kordofan, which is controlled by the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) that have been at war with Sudan’s military since April 2023. Residents and medical workers said a drone struck a transport hub where villagers had gathered after a market day to find rides home, killing 80 people. Ahmed Abakar Wadi, a resident who helped bury victims, told AFP at least 50 bodies were recovered at the scene, including that of his brother. Another 47 wounded people were taken to the nearby town of Al-Mujlad where 30 later died from their injuries, according to a medical source. “The drone struck once, and then came back 10 minutes later and struck again,” Wadi told AFP. The RSF’s self-declared administration, known as Tasis, and the Sudanese rights group Emergency Lawyers accused the army of carrying out the attack. The military has not commented. The strike was one of the deadliest single attacks in Kordofan, an oil-rich region linking western and eastern Sudan where the army and the RSF have been battling for territory. item.title: ‘You Cannot Ask Moses To Go Back To Egypt,’ Tinubu Insists No Fuel Subsidy Return
item.description: President Bola Tinubu has reiterated that there will be no return to the fuel subsidy regime, insisting that his administration took a bold and necessary step to reform the country’s economy. Tinubu spoke on Monday during a meeting with the City Boy Movement, a youth-driven political and advocacy group founded to champion his administration’s agenda. “I came, and I removed the subsidy on my first day. Nigeria would have gone bankrupt; there was nothing left to pay for subsidies,” he said. “I could listen to my political opponents promising a return to subsidy.” Drawing a religious analogy, the president added, “I remember my scripture studies, both in the Bible and the Holy Quran. When Moses (Musa) left Egypt, the Red Sea parted and gave way. You cannot ask Moses to go back to Egypt. With your energy and support, we will never go back to Egypt.” The former Lagos State governor commended the organisation for drumming up support for his administration and urged members to take his government’s achievements to the grassroots. “Those of you who are lucky to work with me have given me all the answers needed and the confidence required to see the coming election as a simple matter,” Tinubu stated. “You will go to your campuses, your markets, and your villages. Make sure every young person you know has a PVC and uses it. Tell them what we have done and tell them what we will do. Campaign with your ideas.” President Tinubu announced an end to fuel subsidy during his inauguration in May 2023. The policy shift sparked an immediate hike in petrol pump prices, rising from under ₦200 per litre to current rates hovering between ₦1,350 and ₦1,405 per litre across major filling stations. While the policy has drawn widespread criticism over the heightened cost of living, the president remains firm on his stance. The federal government maintains that the decision is essential to reset the national economy, reassuring citizens that the initial economic hardship will ease over time.
